title: Appeals court says Trump is unlawfully constructing White House ballroom | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

A dividedfederal appeals court ruled Fridaythat President Donald Trump is unlawfully constructing a massive new ballroom at the White House, teeing up a high-stakes showdown over the issue before the Supreme Court.

“Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help,” the DC Circuit Court of Appeals said in a 2-1 ruling siding with the nation’s top historic preservation group, which sued over the project last year.

“The National Trust has shown, compellingly, that Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House – the People’s House – to fit a particular President’s desires,” the court wrote in its unsigned opinion.

The DC Circuit, however, paused implementation of its ruling for two weeks to give Trump time to appeal to the Supreme Court,which the president said later Friday he intends to do.

“We will be immediately appealing to the United States Supreme Court,” Trump wroteon Truth Social, calling on the nation’s highest court to overturn the decision “in its entirety.”

The judges who ruled against Trump are Patricia Millett, an appointee of former President Barack Obama, and Brad Garcia, an appointee of former President Joe Biden. Judge Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee, dissented.

The majority opinion — spanning more than 100 pages — is the latest stinging judicial rebuke in the legal saga over Trump’s decision to demolish the White House’s East Wing last year to make room for the ballroom.

The ballroom case is also one of several legal challenges brought against Trump’s various pet projects around the District. Other lawsuits calling into question his renovation of the Reflecting Pool, his push to build an American version of Paris’ Arc de Triomphe and his plans to turn a public golf course into private, high-end links are ongoing.

In April, a federal judge in Washington, DC,ordered Trump to stop with all above-ground constructionof the ballroom until Congress blessed his plans. But the appeals court permitted him to continue with the project for now while the court considered the case. Friday’s ruling unwinds that earlier decision and makes clear that the entire project requires congressional approval.

“This is a great day for our country and for the American people’s right to voice their opinions about the historic places they cherish, including the White House,” Brent Leggs, the president and CEO of the National Trust, said in a statement.

Rao said in her dissent that she thought the National Trust did not have the legal right – known as “standing” – to bring the case in the first place, agreeing with arguments pushed by Trump’s lawyers since last year.

She criticized US District Judge Richard Leon, who first ruled against the project last spring, for elevating “the aesthetic displeasure” of the group with the project over Trump’s argument that it’s needed for national security reasons.

“The district court seized supervision of construction at the White House, and my colleagues affirm this judicial overreach,” Rao wrote.

Above-grade construction on the ballroom began in the spring and has made considerable progress. Imagespostedby Trump earlier this week reveal multiple levels of concrete support columns and metal rebar amid a significant amount of construction equipment, including a tower crane.

The president has been personally involved in ballroom details, from floor plans to marble selection. The sprawling ballroom project has an estimated size of approximately 89,000 square feet, according to lead architect Shalom Baranes. By contrast, the primary White House structure, the Executive Mansion, is just 55,000 square feet.

Trump has maintained that the project isn’t subject to any oversight and that he should be able to continue with it without any serious scrutiny. He has said it will be finished in the summer of 2028, an expedited timeline for completion months before he leaves office.

Trump described the 2-1 ruling Friday as “horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful” and suggested that it was “a National Security threat to our Nation” that “severely jeopardizes the lives and welfare of the people who work, and will be working, at the White House.”

The ballroom is being built atop ahighly secretive underground bunker complexaimed at modernizing aging underground infrastructure, which the president said on Friday was “being built for the protection of our Country and, additionally, all future Presidents.”

In his Truth Social post, Trump pointed to some of the features of the underground facility, including “Bomb Shelters, State of the Art Hospital and Medical Facilities, Protective Partitioning, Top Secret Military Facilities, Structures and Equipment, Protective Missile Resistant Steel, Columns, Roofs, and Beams, Drone Proof Ceilings and Roofs, Military Grade Venting, and Bullet, Ballistic, and Blast Proof Glass.”

He also suggested that the ballroom was “a Gift from President Trump and Great Patriots of the United States of America.” However, his administration has sought hundreds of millions of dollars in congressional funding for the project.

In its ruling Friday, the appeals court said, as Leon had, that Trump could continue with work on the below-ground bunker even while construction of the above-ground ballroom is paused.

Millett and Garcia stressed that the president could, for example, “put a fully protective covering over the underground construction and other exposed portions of the construction site” to ensure the bunker isn’t unprotected.

As a Justice Department attorney defending the project pressed the appeals court in June to reverse Leon’s ruling, he pushed an expansive view of executive power that included an assertion that no court had authority to halt construction, even if it was deemed unlawful.

“If this were complete lawlessness by the government, it couldn’t be stopped?” Millett asked, to which the lawyer, Yaakov Roth, replied: “On these theories, I think that’s right.”

In its opinion Friday, the court said that position is flatly wrong.

“The bold assertion that the Executive can act with utter lawlessness, destroying treasured national landmarks and harming the interests of individuals, and that no court can stop it flouts our constitutional order,” the judges in the majority said.

This story has been updated with additional details.
